body.heading: Four squares run the board
paragraphs: Ask strong chess players what the opening is about and most will give the same answer: the centre - the four squares e4, d4, e5 and d5. A piece standing in the centre reaches in every direction. A knight on a central square attacks eight squares; the same knight stuck in a corner attacks only two. Central pieces are simply worth more because they can get to where the action is.

Control does not always mean occupation. You can rule the centre with pawns planted on it, or influence it from a distance with pieces and pawns aiming at it. But every opening system ever invented, from the oldest to the most modern computer-approved line, is in the end an argument about those four squares.

body.heading: Principles that follow from the centre
paragraphs: The classic opening principles are really centre principles in disguise. Develop knights and bishops early because they fight for central squares. Move each piece once before moving any twice, because your army needs to join the argument. Castle early to tuck your king away and connect your rooks. And resist bringing your queen out on early adventures - she is easily chased by developing moves that also claim the centre.

A practical habit for beginners: at move ten, pause and count. How many of your pieces and pawns attack the four centre squares, and how many of your opponent's do? That single count predicts the rest of the game surprisingly well, and it gives you a plan - improve your worst-placed piece by aiming it at the middle.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Set up a knight on an empty board and count its moves from a corner, from an edge, and from the centre - 2, 4 and 8. Do the same for a bishop on a long diagonal versus a short one. Feeling those numbers once teaches more than reading 'centralise your pieces' a dozen times.

Then play a training game where both players agree to note, at move ten, who controls the centre. Win or lose, compare notes afterwards: the player with the centre usually had the easier game, and now you know what to fight for next time.

takeaway: Central pieces reach more of the board, so chess begins as a polite argument about four squares.
